transcript:
**Maester Tomas** (turn 0):
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

**Apprentice** (turn 1):
I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 2):
Tomas set down his stylus with a deliberate click. He removed his spectacles, polished them on the hem of his robe, and replaced them — a ritual that always preceded correction.

"Apprentice Bellen showed you a paper," he repeated, the words flat and cold. "And from that single reading, you now believe you have grounds to contradict the established historical record? How many years of training did Bellen complete before being entrusted with archive access? Two? Three?"

He rose from his chair with the stiff caution of a man whose joints had begun to betray him, and moved to the shelf where the bound histories stood in chronological order. He drew out a volume — heavy, leather-spined, its pages marbled with age — and dropped it on the reading desk with a thud that stirred dust from the vellum.

"Page three hundred and twelve. The Treaty of Veyros, signed by King Aldric II in the presence of six witnesses and the Archmagus of the Conclave. The ink has been authenticated. The seal has been verified. I myself examined the document thirty years ago, when my eyes were still worth something." He jabbed a finger at the apprentice's notes. "What you read in Bellen's paper — and I have read it, do not imagine otherwise — is a *reinterpretation* of correspondence that the western archivists themselves admit is fragmentary. Speculation. Hypothesis. Not fact."

He leaned forward, lowering his voice.

"A treaty *proposed* is not a treaty *signed*. The distinction matters, and if you cannot grasp it now, you will never be a proper scholar. Return to your cataloging. And if Bellen has time to waste pulling speculative papers from restricted stacks, I shall have a word with his master about his curriculum."

**Apprentice** (turn 3):
*I wince slightly as he raises his voice, but I don't back down.* "But Maester, the paper wasn't just speculation. It included newly discovered battle reports from the Northern marches. They describe skirmishes well after 847, involving known mages from the conflict." *I tap my own notes with a nervous finger.* "Wouldn't that suggest the war was, at the very least, still active in some capacity?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 4):
Tomas's mouth thinned into a colorless line. For a moment the only sound in the archive was the settling of old wood and the faint guttering of the candle.

"'Active in some capacity,'" he echoed, each syllable bitten off clean. "There is your error, Apprentice. You have allowed an apprentice's paper to substitute its vocabulary for yours. A war is not 'active in some capacity.' A war is a formal state of organized hostility between recognized powers, waged under declared or understood terms. Skirmishes are skirmishes. Raids are raids. Rogue elements operating without the sanction of the Conclave — which, I will remind you, was *bound* by the Treaty of Veyros from 847 onward — do not constitute a continuation of the Third Magical War any more than a bandit on the Kingsroad makes the realm still at war with the Tsarvani Empire."

He turned back to the shelf, though his hand hovered, not reaching for any volume. His spectacles caught the candlelight as he spoke over his shoulder.

"The northern marches have *always* produced skirmish reports. Cold country. Long border. Disgruntled veterans with grudges and half-trained hedge-mages peddling curses for coin. You will find such reports in 812, in 803, in 779. Shall we un-sign every treaty back to the Second Era because some fool with a staff lit a farmhouse on fire?"

His voice dropped again — not softer, but tighter, the way a man speaks when he is choosing his words with surgical care.

"I have read Bellen's paper. I read it when it was first unsealed, and I read it again last winter. The battle reports he cites are three in number — three, out of forty-four years. Two of them name no mage of any Conclave rank. The third names a field-apprentice whose master had already been executed for war crimes in 845." He turned back, fixing the apprentice with a look that was not unkind but absolutely immovable. "Bellen is a bright boy. He has found a fragment of a fragment and built a cathedral of speculation upon it. That is not scholarship. That is ambition mistaking itself for discovery."

He retrieved his stylus and sat back down, though his hand did not resume its tracing.

"You will catalog the Veyrosi correspondence. And if you wish to understand why a *signed* treaty is not undone by three scattered reports of rogue magic in the boondocks of the north, you will read the actual treaty text — not Bellen's commentary on it — and then you will write me a précis on the difference between a state of war and a state of *peace imperfectly maintained*." The stylus tapped once against the desk. "Due tomorrow. First bell."

**Apprentice** (turn 5):
*I sigh, deflating a bit.* "Yes, Maester." *I walk over to the Veyrosi correspondence, pulling out the first scroll and unrolling it carefully. I guess I'll be up late tonight.*

**Maester Tomas** (turn 6):
Tomas watched the apprentice unroll the scroll with hands that were, he noted with grim satisfaction, reasonably careful. At least the child knew how to handle vellum. Some small mercy.

He turned back to his own manuscript, but the lines of ink seemed to swim before him more than usual. He frowned, adjusted his spectacles, and held the page closer to the candle. The words did not improve.

"Apprentice," he said, without looking up. "When you reach the fourth scroll in the bundle — the one with the broken seal — bring it to me first. The wax has the Conclave stamp, but I suspect it is a forgery from the Second Era reused as binding. If I am correct, there will be a hairline crack along the griffin's wing where the original impression was ground down." He paused, the stylus hovering. "And Apprentice."

The word hung in the air, waiting.

"It is not that Bellen is wrong to *ask* the question. Scholarship requires that questions be asked." His stylus resumed its tracing, though his hand moved more slowly than before. "It is that Bellen has not yet learned the difference between asking a question and answering one. When you have been in these archives as long as I have, you will understand: the dangerous thing is not the contradiction. The dangerous thing is a young man with a single document and absolute certainty."

The candle sputtered. Tomas did not look up.

"First bell tomorrow. I do not accept late précis."

**Apprentice** (turn 7):
"But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

**Maester Tomas** (turn 8):
Tomas's stylus stopped mid-trace. For a long moment he did not move. Then, with the slow deliberation of a man reining in his temper, he set the stylus down and turned in his chair.

"Show me."

The apprentice extended the copy. Tomas took it between ink-stained fingers, holding it at arm's length, then closer, then at an angle to the candlelight. His lips moved as he read. The silence stretched.

"A war decree," he said at last, the words precise and quiet. "You have read this document. Tell me — what precisely does it *say*? Word for word, if you can manage it. What is decreed?"

He did not wait for an answer. He set the copy flat on the desk and pressed a fingertip to the date line.

"'A war decree.' You have taken a single noun and built your entire argument upon it. You have not told me whether this document mobilizes a levy, declares hostilities, invokes the Conclave's dissolution, or simply authorizes the Crown's garrisons to continue their standing patrols along the northern marches." His finger tapped the parchment. "Because those are *very different things*, Apprentice. A king may issue a thousand military documents in a year and not one of them need be a declaration of war."

He straightened, removing his spectacles and pinching the bridge of his nose.

"I will tell you what I suspect this document is, because I have read dozens like it. It is a routine authorization — likely a continuation order for the northern garrison, or a commission for a specific officer, or a requisition of supplies for a border watch. Aldric II reigned for *thirty-six years* after Veyros. Do you imagine the man issued no military correspondence in all that time? That the moment the ink dried on the treaty, the Crown's war-chancellery shuttered its doors and the clerks took up embroidery?"

His spectacles came back down. He looked at the apprentice with eyes that, though failing, missed nothing.

"Furthermore. You say this document bears the king's seal. Very well. The royal seal was applied to *thousands* of documents in any given year — patents, writs, proclamations, pardons, land grants, tax assessments. Its presence proves only that the document passed through the Crown's chancery. It does not prove the document *re-opened a war.*"

He pushed the copy back across the desk.

"Return this to Bellen. And tell him — since you are evidently to be his messenger in this — that if he wishes to overturn thirty years of authenticated scholarship, he will need more than one routine military document with the wrong noun attached to it. He will need the *suppression* of the original treaty. He will need a witness or a counter-signatory contradicting the six already on record. He will need to explain why the Archmagus, who lived until 871, never once in his surviving correspondence suggests the war continued."

The candle guttered. Tomas held a hand over it, shielding the flame, and his voice dropped — not to softness, but to the low register he used when he was past irritation and into something colder.

"I have been in these archives thirty years, Apprentice. I have read every scrap of the Veyrosi correspondence. I have handled the treaty itself. I knew the Archmagus's last secretary personally — a tiresome woman, but meticulous to the point of madness. If the war had continued, there would be traces. There would be *hundreds* of traces. There are not." He paused. "Bellen has found a puddle and called it an ocean. That is not your concern. Your concern is the fourth scroll, the broken seal, and a précis due at first bell."

He turned back to his manuscript. His hand resumed its tracing. But after a moment, almost as an afterthought:

"And Apprentice. The phrase is *'northern marches,'* not *'Northern Marches.'* The distinction matters. One is a region. The other is a formal marcher lordship. If you cannot manage capitalization, you will not manage the précis."

**Apprentice** (turn 9):
*I retrieve the copy, my face a little flushed.* "Yes, Maester. I... I understand." *I turn back to the Veyrosi correspondence, making sure to capitalize "Northern Marches" in my head as I re-read the first scroll.*

**Maester Tomas** (turn 10):
Tomas did not respond immediately. The stylus resumed its slow passage across the manuscript, though whether he was truly reading or merely tracing the habit of decades was difficult to say. The candle had burned low; he reached for the snuffers without looking, pinched the flame to a stub, and relit it from a second taper kept by his elbow. The new flame steadied the shadows but did nothing for the swimming of the ink.

He turned a page of his manuscript. Then another. The apprentice, behind him, was making the soft sounds of careful unrolling — no tearing, no scraping of vellum against the desk's edge. Acceptable.

After some minutes, Tomas spoke without turning.

"The first scroll you are handling now is a letter from the Archmagus's third secretary to a Veyrosi clerk. It concerns a shipment of bound grimoires the Conclave was surrendering to the Crown's custody. Note the date. Note the language of *surrender.* When I was your age, I misread that letter three times before a senior maester pointed out that the vocabulary alone settles the question of the treaty's status. A Conclave surrendering grimoires is not a Conclave still at war." The stylus tapped once,

**Apprentice** (turn 11):
"So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

**Maester Tomas** (turn 12):
Tomas set down his stylus. He did not turn around, but the apprentice could see the slow rise of his shoulders, the way his ink-stained fingers pressed flat against the manuscript page as though anchoring himself to the desk.

"'The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another,'" he repeated, his voice measured in the particular way that meant the storm had not yet broken. "'What's the truth.' As though you have placed two documents of equal weight upon a scale and are waiting for me to tip it for you."

He turned in his chair. The candlelight caught the deep grooves around his mouth, the gray that had long since eaten his beard, the spectacles that sat slightly crooked on a nose too prominent for them.

"I will tell you what the truth is, Apprentice, since you have asked so prettily. The truth is that you have been *misusing the word 'evidence.'*"

He held up a finger.

"Evidence is not a thing that becomes more or less true according to when it was found. A treaty signed in the presence of six witnesses — whose ink has been authenticated, whose seal has been verified, which has been cited in *every* subsequent legal instrument between Crown and Conclave for half a century — is not undone by a fragmentary battle report dug out of a western archive a decade ago. The *age* of a document has nothing to do with its *authority.*"

He rose again, moving to the shelf, and drew out a slim volume bound in pale leather — a concordance of treaties, heaped with marginalia in a dozen hands.

"Open this. Read the entry for Veyros. Note the cross-references. The Crown's subsequent land grants to the Conclave. The Conclave's own internal correspondence acknowledging the treaty's terms. The tax exemptions granted to mage-towers in 858, 862, 867 — *after* your supposed war decree, Apprentice. A Conclave at war is not collecting tax exemptions. A Conclave at war is not *accepting* tax exemptions."

He set the concordance down beside the apprentice's work, open to the relevant page.

"'The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.' No. The *textbook* says what the evidence supports. Bellen's paper says what a single fragment *speculates.* You do not weigh a cathedral against a brick and call the scale balanced. You do not dismiss a signed treaty because an apprentice in the western archives has found three skirmish reports that *might* involve rogue mages operating without the sanction of the very body that *signed* the treaty."

His hand came down on the concordance, not hard, but firm.

"The treaty is real. The war ended in 847 AE. Every authenticated document in this archive — and there are *hundreds* — supports this. Bellen has offered us a handful of fragments and a theory. A theory is not evidence. A theory is what you *build* when you do not yet have evidence."

He straightened, fixing the apprentice with that look again — not unkind, but absolutely immovable.

"And that, Apprentice, will be the subject of your précis. Not 'what is the truth,' as though truth were a thing one stumbled upon by accident. But *how one distinguishes between an authenticated record and a speculative reinterpretation.* You will give me your answer, in writing, with citations, at first bell tomorrow. If you cannot cite at least six independent documents supporting the treaty's validity, you will return to the stacks and try again."

He turned back to his manuscript, then paused.

"The concordance. *Read* it before you catalog the next scroll. And if I find a single instance of you referring to Bellen's paper as 'new evidence' in your précis, I will have you copying the entire Veyrosi correspondence by hand. Every letter. Both sides. The quill will be the smallest I can find."

The stylus resumed its tracing. Tomas did not look up.

"First bell, Apprentice. Do not be late."

**Apprentice** (turn 13):
*I stare at the concordance, then at the maester's back. I guess I'm not getting out of this précis.* "Yes, Maester. I understand. I'll... I'll get to it." *I pull the concordance closer, flipping to the page he indicated.*

**Maester Tomas** (turn 14):
Tomas did not look up as the apprentice settled into the concordance. The soft turning of pages was, he supposed, better than the sound of argument. He let several minutes pass in silence, the only motion in the archive the slow crawl of his stylus across his own manuscript and the occasional settling of old wood.

Then, without warning:

"You are turning too many pages at once. The vellum will crack along the gutter if you treat it like a chapbook. One page. Lift from the lower corner. *Always* the lower corner."

The stylus traced another line. The apprentice corrected their handling. Tomas noted it, said nothing further, and returned to his work.

Minutes more. The candle burned lower. Outside, the first stars had begun to prick the dark above the northern windows, and the archive had taken on that particular hush of late evening — when the building itself seemed to draw breath and hold it.

"I knew a man once," Tomas said abruptly, his voice so quiet the apprentice had to lean forward to catch it, "who spent fourteen years building a case that the Second Era began not in 612 AE but in 617. He had documents. He had witnesses. He had a theory so elegant it could make a scholar weep." The stylus paused. "He was wrong. Every authenticated source contradicted him, but he had made the theory his life's work, and so he could not let it go. He died still arguing. His name is not remembered for his discovery. It is not remembered at all."

He let the silence stretch.

"I am not telling you this as a warning, Apprentice. I am telling you this because in thirty years you will meet that man again, and again, and again — in yourself, if you are not careful. Scholars are not paid to be *certain.* They are paid to be *rigorous.* Certainty is for kings and fools."

He turned a page of his manuscript. The wax tablet on his desk bore a list of names in his own cramped hand; he glanced at it, frowned, and crossed one out with a single deliberate stroke.

"Your précis. When you write it. You will not begin with the battle reports. You will begin with the treaty itself — the parchment, the ink, the witnesses. You will describe what a signed document *is* and what it *does.* Only then will you turn to the fragments Bellen has gathered, and you will explain, with citations, why they do not outweigh the record." He glanced over his spectacles at the apprentice. "If you begin with the fragments, you will spend the entire précis justifying them, and you will lose the architecture of the argument. Architecture is everything. A précis is not a confession. It is a *building.*"

He turned back to his manuscript, then stopped, the stylus hovering.

"And Apprentice."

The word hung in the candlelit air.

"If, when you have written it, you find that you cannot honestly support the position I have outlined — that the evidence, as you weigh it, does not permit the conclusion I have asked of you — you will bring that précis to me *anyway.* Don't dress it as something it is not. Don't sand the corners off your doubts to make me comfortable." His voice dropped, almost to a murmur. "A maester who cannot tolerate an honest disagreement is not a maester. He is a clerk with pretensions. I have been a clerk with pretensions. I would not wish it on you."

He resumed his tracing.

"Now. The concordance. *Carefully.*"

**Apprentice** (turn 15):
*I nod slowly, absorbing his words. That last part... that was unexpected. I turn back to the concordance, carefully turning a page.* "Yes, Maester. Carefully."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 16):
The archive settled into the particular quiet of deep evening. Tomas worked in silence for a span that might have been a quarter of an hour or might have been longer — time moved strangely in the stacks, when the candles burned and no bells marked the hours. His stylus traced its slow path across the manuscript, pausing occasionally as his failing eyes required him to bring the page closer to the light. Twice he muttered something under his breath — corrections, most likely, for a text that would not behave.

At length he set the stylus down, pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes for a moment, and exhaled through his nose.

"Apprentice. Bring me the fourth scroll. We will examine the seal together, since you are already at the correspondence." He did not look up. "And bring the lamp, not the candle. The candle throws the light at the wrong angle for seal-work. You will need to see the hairline along the griffin's wing, and a guttering flame will only make you imagine things that are not there."

He cleared a space on his desk — sweeping aside his own manuscript with a care that suggested the pages were in no particular order he wished disturbed — and waited. When the apprentice brought the scroll and the lamp, he took both with the unhurried deliberation of a man who had handled a thousand such objects and intended to handle a thousand more.

"Set the lamp here. Angle it so the light rakes across the wax, not into it. You want the shadows to fall along any crack, not across it." He waited until the apprentice had adjusted the lamp, then produced from his sleeve a small lens — not the spectacles he wore, but a stronger one, mounted in a bone frame. He held it close to the broken seal and bent until his nose nearly touched the wax.

"Here." He did not point; he waited for the apprentice to draw near. "Tell me what you see at the griffin's wing. Specifically at the joint — where the foreleg meets the body."

He waited, breathing slowly through his mouth as he always did when concentrating, the smell of old wax and older vellum filling the archive around them. Whatever the apprentice reported, Tomas would respond to it — with correction, or with confirmation, or with the kind of dry commentary that suggested the apprentice had seen precisely what he had hoped they would not.

"And while you look," he added, almost as an afterthought, "consider this: a maester who cannot recognize a forgery is a maester who cannot recognize a *fact.* The two skills are not so different as the young scholars believe. Both require you to look at a thing and resist the temptation to see what you *expect* to see."

**Apprentice** (turn 17):
*I lean in close, angling my head to catch the light just right. My eyes dart to the griffin's wing, trying to find what he's talking about.* "I... I think I see it, Maester. There's a faint line, almost like a scratch, right where the wing connects. It's very thin."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 18):
Tomas did not move for a long moment. The lens stayed pressed close to the wax, his breath held, the lamplight raking across the griffin's wing at the precise angle he had demanded. Then, slowly, he lowered the lens and sat back.

"Good."

The word was not warm. It was not even, precisely, praise. It was acknowledgment — the kind a maester gives when an apprentice has finally done the thing they were asked to do, no more and no less. Tomas set the lens on the desk with a small click and looked at the apprentice directly.

"Almost like a scratch," he repeated. "You see the hesitation in your own observation, which is the correct hesitation. It is *not* a scratch. A scratch would be irregular — deeper at one end, shallower at the other, perhaps with a curl of displaced wax. What you have found is a *straight* line, uniform in depth, terminating cleanly at both ends. That is the mark of a tool — a stylus or a fine blade, drawn deliberately across the surface to flatten an older impression."

He turned back to the scroll, angling the lamp slightly to catch the line from another direction.

"Observe also: the original impression — the one beneath — would have been a Conclave stamp of an *earlier* design. The griffin in this seal has a single plume on its crest. The Conclave stamp used after the Schism of 731 AE bears a *double* plume. So the underlying impression is pre-Schism, and the forger ground it down to reuse the wax — either to bind a document of the Second Era, or to lend the *appearance* of authority to something newer." His finger traced the air above the crack without touching it. "You cannot, from this seal alone, determine which. That requires the document itself. But the seal tells you *this* seal cannot be trusted as evidence of a Conclave authentication in the period of the Third Magical War."

He straightened, removing his spectacles and rubbing the bridge of his nose.

"Now. Consider what you have just done." His voice took on the cadence of a lecture, though he did not rise or turn to address the apprentice formally. "You looked at an object. You resisted the temptation to declare it authentic because it *looked* like a Conclave seal. You looked for what was *actually there* — not what you expected to see, not what would have been convenient for your argument, but what the wax itself showed you under proper light. You found a crack. You described it accurately — *almost like a scratch* — which is to say, you described it as a thing you had actually observed, rather than a thing you had decided was true."

He replaced his spectacles.

"That is the same skill, Apprentice. Whether the object before you is a wax seal or a piece of parchment bearing a king's name. The discipline does not change. You look. You describe what is there. You resist the impulse to make the evidence *agree* with you." A pause. The candle on the far desk guttered; Tomas ignored it. "Bellen failed at that step. He looked at three battle reports and decided they were evidence of a continuing war, when — by his own admission in the paper's third appendix — none of them name the Conclave as a participant, none of them cite any authorization from the Archmagus, and all of them occur in regions where the Crown had standing garrison orders for routine border security."

He tapped the lens once against the desk.

"You, however. You looked at a seal and saw a crack. That is the foundation of everything else we do in this archive. Do not forget it." He lifted the lens and tucked it back into his sleeve. "Now. We will examine the document the seal binds. I suspect — though I will not declare it until we have read — that the letter inside is a genuine Second Era correspondence that someone in a later century bound with a forged Conclave seal to lend it weight. A common enough fraud. If I am right, the handwriting inside will not match Second Era chancery script, and you will be able to tell me *why* it does not match."

He pushed the scroll gently toward the apprentice.

"Unroll it. Carefully. From the *lower* edge. And tell me what you see before you tell me what you *think* you see."

**Apprentice** (turn 19):
*I carefully unroll the scroll from the lower edge, my eyes scanning the faded script. I pull out my own magnifying glass, a much simpler one, and compare the writing to the examples in my head.* "Maester, the script... it's a mix. Some of the letters are very formal, almost like the Second Era examples, but then others are more fluid, almost cursive. It's like two different people wrote it, or someone was trying to imitate an older style and sometimes slipped up."

**Maester Tomas** (turn 20):
Tomas's hand, which had been reaching for the concordance, stopped. He turned back toward the apprentice, and for a moment his expression was unreadable — the candlelight catching the deep lines of his face, the spectacles still slightly askew on his nose.

Then, very quietly, he said: "Again."

He rose from his chair and moved to stand beside the apprentice at the desk, bringing the lamp with him. He did not ask permission to take the scroll; he simply adjusted its angle under the light with the practiced hand of a man who had positioned ten thousand such documents in his lifetime.

"Show me."

The apprentice indicated the passage where the formal script gave way to the fluid. Tomas held his bone-framed lens over the transition point and bent close, his beard nearly brushing the vellum. He did not speak for a long moment.

Then he straightened.

"'Two different people wrote it, or someone was trying to imitate an older style and sometimes slipped up.'" He set the lens down with a deliberate care. "That is a *description*, Apprentice. It is not yet an *observation.*"

He drew the lamp closer and pointed — not at the script itself, but at the space between two lines, where a single descender had trailed downward into the margin.

"Here. Look at this descender. The *r* in — what is this word, *'coram'*? The *r* begins in the formal chancery manner: a vertical stroke, a small loop at the top, a controlled curve at the foot. But it *terminates* in a flourish — a long, sweeping tail that runs nearly a full line-height below the baseline. That flourish is *not* Second Era chancery script. Second Era chancery terminates descenders with a small hook, never a sweep. The sweep is characteristic of post-Reformation court hands — specifically, the *Aldricine* style that emerged in the second decade of Aldric II's reign."

His finger moved along the line.

"Here. And here. Two more descenders in this single sentence, both with the Aldricine sweep. The verticals are *mimicked* formal — the scribe knew what Second Era chancery *looked* like, and reproduced the upper portions correctly. But the *habits of the hand* — the flourishes the writer could not help but make — betray him. He is not imitating an older style and 'slipping up,' as you so charmingly put it. He is *copying* an older style with one part of his mind while the other part *writes naturally.* That is what every forger does. The question is never whether the forger knows the older style — often they do, and very well. The question is whether the forger can *unlearn* his own."

He tapped the lens against the desk — a habit, the apprentice was beginning to realize, that punctuated his thoughts the way a hammer punctuated a stave.

"You said 'two different people.' That is a possibility. It is the *lazier* possibility, and a maester who reaches for it first is a maester who will be fooled often. Consider: if two scribes had collaborated on this letter, one in formal chancery and one in Aldricine court hand, would they have *alternated mid-sentence?* Would the first scribe have begun the word *'coram'* and the second have completed it? That would be an absurd division of labor. No, Apprentice. One hand. One writer. One mind that knew the older form by *study* and wrote in the newer form by *habit.*"

He turned the scroll, angling it under the lamp.

"Now. The harder question."

His voice dropped — not to softness, but to the particular tone he used when he was about to say something he considered important.

"Where does the forgery begin? You have identified the transition — or what you have *called* a transition. But a maester does not stop at the first sign of trouble. A maester asks: *is this entire document a forgery, or is it a forgery imposed upon a genuine older text?*"

He let the question sit in the archive air, between the candle-smoke and the smell of old wax.

"Observe the opening lines. The salutation. The date formula. Are *those* in pure Second Era chancery, with no Aldricine habits showing through? Or is the *entire* document written by a post-Reformation hand attempting to pass itself off as older?" He glanced at the apprentice. "That is the question that determines whether this letter is *evidence* of anything at all. A forgery of an older text, written by a later scribe, is not a Second Era document. It is a *later document about* the Second Era. And those are very different things, Apprentice. A man in 870 AE writing about the Second Era tells us what *he* believed about the Second Era. He does not tell us what the Second Era *was.*"

He stepped back, giving the apprentice room at the desk.
